title: The Catalyst for the July Revolution

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.dialogue: On 1 July 2024, students gathered on campuses across Bangladesh, including Dhaka University, for calm demonstrations. These protests had just resumed. At this early stage they were peaceful, a long way from the violent crackdown that would come later in July.

scenes.speaker: Narrator
scenes.dialogue: The trigger sat a few weeks earlier. In June 2024, the High Court reinstated a 30 percent government-job quota reserved for descendants of freedom fighters, reversing a 2018 decision that had abolished it. In a country with high youth unemployment, students read the ruling as a narrowing of merit-based opportunities.

evidence.title: A Student Joins the Movement
evidence.sourceCaption: The Christian Science Monitor, "Bangladeshi youth bore the brunt of last week's violent protests. They want accountability," published and updated 26 July 2024. Paraphrased reporting, not a direct quote.
evidence.text: Prapti Taposhi, an economics student at Jahangirnagar University, was among the first students to join the July 2024 protests over the reinstated government job quota.

evidence.title: A Parallel Dispute
evidence.sourceCaption: European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA), Bangladesh Country Focus Country of Origin Information Report, August 2025, "1–3 July 2024: Initial protests" section, citing local media reporting.
evidence.text: Alongside the student protests, teachers at 35 public universities went on strike over changes to their pension scheme, suspending academic and administrative activities indefinitely during the same period in late June and July 2024. Some teachers were therefore engaged in a separate labor dispute with the government while the student quota protests were unfolding on their campuses.
